method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis' (published 19 June 2025). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12778014). The ranked source, the International TSC Consensus Group 2021 recommendations (Pediatric Neurology, CC BY-NC-ND), returned a bot challenge (HTTP 403) on ScienceDirect and is not in PMC, so it was not used. This open narrative review restates the 2021 consensus and the 2024 ERKNet kidney consensus for diagnosis, kidney surveillance and everolimus.

claims.claim: **TSC is a rare autosomal dominant disorder (1:6000–1:10,000 live births) from loss-of-function variants in TSC1 or TSC2,** causing benign tumours in the kidney, brain, skin, heart and lung.
claims.source_text: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder that afflicts 1:6000-1:10,000 live births and is caused by pathologic loss-of-function (LoF) variants in either TSC complex subunit 1 (TSC1) or TSC complex subunit 2 (TSC2)., TSC is characterized by pleomorphic benign tumors of multiple organ systems, including the kidney, brain, skin, heart, and lung.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect TSC with prenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma, infantile spasms or epilepsy, and hypomelanotic skin macules in childhood;** each is non-specific alone. In infancy and childhood TSC most often presents with seizures.
claims.source_text: Clinical suspicion should be heightened in patients with prenatal cardiac rhabdomyoma(s), infantile spasms/epilepsy, and childhood hypomelanotic skin macules. However, each of these clinical features are nonspecific in isolation, and features of TSC may not present simultaneously. … TSC in infancy and childhood most often presents with seizures.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Multifocal angiomyolipomas, especially with kidney cysts, should prompt a search for other TSC criteria.**
claims.source_text: Multifocal AMLs, particularly when associated with kidney cysts, should prompt an evaluation for additional major or minor TSC criteria to establish a diagnosis.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant (ACMG standards) is enough for diagnosis.** Clinically, the 2021 criteria have 11 major and seven minor features; diagnosis needs two major, or one major plus two minor.
claims.source_text: The molecular identification of a pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant by the standards of the American College of Medical Genetics is diagnostically sufficient for TSC. … The clinical criteria of TSC were updated in 2021 and include 11 major criteria and seven minor criteria. A definitive clinical diagnosis is made with either two major features or a combination of one major and two minor features
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Offer genetic testing to people who meet the criteria** (for prognosis and family), though it is not required for diagnosis. The review's authors also test all first-degree relatives, which differs from one expert consensus.
claims.source_text: Although not required for diagnosis, genetic testing should be offered to those who fulfill TSC criteria as a result of prognostic and familial utility. … Genetic testing should be offered to all patients with TSC and to all first-degree relatives of index patients because the identification of a pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant is sufficient for diagnosis. The spatiotemporal variability of disease manifestations, in terms of both patient age and organ involvement, signify the importance of such practice for early diagnosis, surveillance, and management. Although this practice differs from a recent expert consensus statement, which does not recommend the routine genetic analysis of family members of TSC patients with a known pathogenic variant, their recommendation was level D (weak) and conceded that their approach may not be cost-effective.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sequence blood first; if negative, test affected tissue,** because mosaicism is common. Next-generation sequencing finds a variant in >90%.
claims.source_text: For clinically diagnosed patients, NGS of blood is performed to identify pathogenic mutations. If no mutation is detected in blood, targeted genetic testing of affected tissue is recommended to improve diagnostic yield. … Next-generation sequencing increases the sensitivity for low-level mosaicism to detect pathologic TSC1/TSC2 variants in >90% of patients.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not order TSC gene tests without clinical suspicion:** thousands of rare variants occur in adults without TSC, so pathogenicity can be hard to call.
claims.source_text: thousands of rare TSC1 and TSC2 variants have been identified in a large group of adults who are unlikely to have a diagnosis of TSC, such that the determination of pathogenicity may not be straightforward and genetic testing should not be conducted in the absence of clinical suspicion.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Kidney disease is the most common cause of death in adults with TSC.**
claims.source_text: associated kidney disease is the most common cause of death in adults with TSC.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Abdominal MRI at diagnosis and every year,** dropping to every 2–3 years for small lesions (<1 cm) stable for ≥3 years. MRI is preferred over CT (radiation) and ultrasound (misses fat-poor lesions). Keep surveilling even with no lesions yet.
claims.source_text: Expert consensus recommends an abdominal MRI at diagnosis and annually thereafter, with reduced frequency to every 2-3 years for small lesions (<1 cm) that demonstrate chronic stability (≥3 years). As the development of kidney manifestations may be delayed, noting median ages for cyst and AML detection are 3 and 8-13 years, respectively, regular surveillance should not be abandoned even in the absence of kidney lesions. … MRI is the modality of choice because it adequately discerns the soft tissue components of AMLs, noting fat-poor variants may be isoechoic and difficult to visualize by ultrasound while surveillance CTs may lead to significant cumulative radiation exposure.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check kidney function annually from adulthood;** children rarely develop CKD.
claims.source_text: Children with TSC rarely develop CKD, even in the setting of a significant burden of renal lesions, and the monitoring of kidney function can be deferred until annual measurements in adulthood.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Blood pressure yearly;** 24-hour ambulatory monitoring for adolescents and adults with office BP ≥120/70. An ACE inhibitor or ARB is first line.
claims.source_text: A standardized office BP measurement should be conducted annually and a 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring conducted for adolescents and adults with an office BP of ≥120/70. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers are the preferable first-line antihypertensives, irrespective of the presence of proteinuria.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat enlarging angiomyolipomas ≥3 cm pre-emptively,** because lesions ≥4 cm may form aneurysms that rupture.
claims.source_text: As AMLs ≥4 cm may develop aneurysms that rupture, guidelines advise that demonstratably enlarging AMLs of ≥3 cm be preemptively treated.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Everolimus is advised for enlarging angiomyolipomas >3 cm at any age; sirolimus is a reasonable alternative.** Response is usually seen by 3 months, with maximal shrinkage by 6–12 months; safety and efficacy are shown for up to 4 years.
claims.source_text: Everolimus has been studied in this context and has been advised for enlarging AMLs of >3 cm independent of age, whereas sirolimus may be a reasonable alternative. Typically, AMLs responded to mTORC1 inhibitors by 3 months in EXIST-2, and AML volume maximally reduced within 6-12 months. The safety and efficacy of everolimus have been demonstrated for up to 4 years of treatment.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Evidence:** in EXIST-2 (118 adults), everolimus shrank angiomyolipomas ≥3 cm by ≥50% in 42% at 3 months and 55% at 6 months, versus 0% on placebo. In EXIST-1 it reduced SEGA volume by ≥50% in 35% versus 0%.
claims.source_text: In Examining Everolimus in a Study of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (EXIST-2), a multicenter randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial of 118 TSC adults with renal AMLs, treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor everolimus achieved ≥50% reduction in AMLs of ≥3 cm in 42% of participants by 3 months and 55% at 6 months, as compared with 0% in the placebo arm, whereas 80% of patients overall had >30% reduction at 6 months., Meanwhile, in Examining Everolimus in a Study of Tuberous Sclerosis 1, everolimus induced a ≥50% reduction in subependymal giant cell astrocytoma volume in 35% of patients, compared with 0% in placebo.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute haemorrhage (such as Wunderlich syndrome): mTOR inhibitors have no role; renal artery embolisation is preferred over nephrectomy.**
claims.source_text: mTORC1 inhibition is preventative therapy for spontaneous bleeding from AMLs but has no role in the acute management of life-threatening hemorrhage, such as Wunderlich syndrome, with renal artery embolization highly preferred over nephrectomy as the first approach.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor eGFR and proteinuria before starting mTOR inhibitors and every 3–12 months;** they can cause or worsen proteinuria.
claims.source_text: mTORC1 inhibitor therapy can induce or exacerbate proteinuria, which may become refractory with extended treatment, such that eGFR and proteinuria should be checked before starting treatment and monitored every 3-12 months.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider biopsy for angiomyolipomas growing >0.5 cm a year,** especially if they do not respond to mTOR inhibition, since fat-poor lesions can mimic renal cell carcinoma.
claims.source_text: histologic sampling may be restricted to AMLs manifesting rapid and sustained growth of >0.5 cm per year, particularly those which do not respond to mTORC1 inhibition.
claims.locator: Robichaud JH, Afrin H, Torres VE, Gupta NR (Mayo Clinic), Kidney360 vol 6 issue 10 p1818, doi 10.34067/KID.0000000904, 'Clinical Management of Tuberous Sclerosis', published 19 June 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12778014/, retrieved 2026-09-23
